pos: n. (Maximus the Confessor, c. 580–662, monk and theologian, chief opponent of Monothelitism, mutilated and exiled for refusing the imperial compromise on the two wills of Christ)
etymology: Latin Maximus, greatest; the title Confessor is given in the East to one who suffered for the faith without being put to death.
biblical_def: Maximus the Confessor stood almost alone against an emperor, a patriarch and a pope. The seventh-century court, hoping to win back the Monophysite provinces, proposed that Christ has two natures but one will — Monothelitism — and published it as imperial doctrine. Maximus saw that this emptied Chalcedon: a nature without a will is not a complete nature, and if Christ has no human will then He has no complete humanity, and the obedience by which we are saved was never rendered as man. His proof text is Gethsemane. “Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done” (Luk 22:42) names two wills in one speaker, the human submitting to the divine. Joh 6:38 says the same: “I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me.” Heb 4:15 requires a real human nature tempted in all points. For this Maximus was tried, his tongue cut out and his right hand struck off so that he could neither speak nor write the faith, and he was sent to die in Lazica. The Third Council of Constantinople vindicated him in 681, nineteen years after his death.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the will as that faculty of the mind by which we determine either to do or forbear an action; the faculty which is exercised in deciding.
webster_full: WILL, n. That faculty or endowment of the soul by which it determines either to do or forbear an action.
2. Choice; determination.
That which is strongly desired or intended; purpose; design.
scriptures: Saying, Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.
Joh 6:38
For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me.
And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
Heb 4:15
For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
corruption_summary: Monothelitism was proposed as a reasonable compromise to heal a schism, which is how the church learns that a compromise on Christ heals nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: The imperial doctrine was not a wicked invention; it was a peace plan. The eastern provinces were lost to Monophysitism and the empire needed them, and one will seemed a small price. Maximus answered that it was not a small price but the whole price, because a Christ who lacks a human will lacks a human nature, and the active obedience of a true man is precisely what the gospel requires. The lesson outlasts the controversy: every generation is offered doctrinal concession as the cost of unity, and Gal 2:5 is the apostolic reply — “To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.”

A second caution concerns the use made of Maximus today. He is the favourite father of modern Eastern Orthodoxy and is quarried for a scheme of deification in which the creature is drawn up into the divine energies, and for a cosmic reading of salvation that goes well beyond anything Scripture states. Honour his Christology, which is Chalcedon defended at the cost of his tongue and his hand, and decline his speculative anthropology. The believer is united to Christ, adopted, justified and sanctified, and shall be glorified; he does not become what God is.

“not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me” (Joh 6:38) — the human will submitting.
“was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin” (Heb 4:15) — a complete humanity required.

pos: n. (Theodore of Mopsuestia, c. 350–428, bishop of Mopsuestia, the greatest exegete of the Antiochene school and the teacher behind Nestorius; condemned at Constantinople in 553)
etymology: Greek Theodoros, gift of God; Mopsuestia was a city of Cilicia, the hearth of Mopsus.
biblical_def: Theodore of Mopsuestia was called in his own lifetime simply the Interpreter. Trained under Diodore of Tarsus with John Chrysostom as his fellow student, he brought to the text a historical and grammatical discipline that stands in sharp contrast to Alexandrian allegory: he asked what the human author said, in what circumstances, to whom, and he refused to find a hidden sense where the words gave a plain one. That method is right, and much of what is sound in Protestant exegesis descends from it. But he applied it with a flat literalism that cost him the unity of Scripture. He denied that most of the messianic psalms speak of Christ at all, assigning them to Hezekiah or to the psalmist's own troubles, and so set aside the rule Christ Himself gave in Luk 24:27, where “beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself,” and in Joh 5:46, “he wrote of me.” His Christology divided the Person as his exegesis divided the canon, and Nestorius drew the conclusion his master had made available.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exegesis as explanation; exposition; and to interpret as to explain the meaning of words or writings.
webster_full: EX'EGESIS, n. Explanation; exposition.
INTER'PRET, v.t. To explain the meaning of words to a person who does not understand them; to expound; to translate into intelligible or familiar language.
2. To explain or unfold the meaning of predictions, prophecies, or any thing not plain.
scriptures: And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
Joh 5:46
For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me.
Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.
Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
corruption_summary: Theodore shows that a right method pressed without the Lord's own rule of reading yields a Bible with no Christ in the Old Testament.
corruption_paragraphs: The grammatical-historical method is the correct one, and this dictionary uses it. Theodore's failure was not method but the refusal of a datum the method must receive: that the Spirit who inspired the prophets was testifying beforehand of Christ. 1Pe 1:11 says the prophets searched what “the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ.” A reading that honours the human author and denies the divine Author's intent is not more historical, only less complete. Modern historical criticism inherits Theodore's half and has made a discipline of it, producing an Old Testament about Israel alone.

The opposite corruption is the allegorism Theodore was right to resist, in which any text may be made to say anything by a spiritual sense the words do not bear. 2Pe 1:20 forbids it: “no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.” The recovery lies between, and Christ gave it on the Emmaus road: the plain sense of the words, read in the whole canon, with Himself as the subject the Scriptures were written to declare. Typology that the New Testament actually draws is not allegory, and refusing it is not sobriety.

“for he wrote of me” (Joh 5:46) — Moses as a witness to Christ.

pos: n. (Diodore of Tarsus, d. c. 390, bishop of Tarsus and founder of the Antiochene school of interpretation, teacher of John Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia)
etymology: Greek Diodoros, gift of Zeus; Tarsus in Cilicia, the city of the apostle Paul.
biblical_def: Diodore of Tarsus led the ascetic school at Antioch that trained the two greatest preachers and expositors of the next generation, and he set its principle: the interpreter must give the sense the words bear, in their history and order, and must not substitute a spiritual meaning for the plain one. He wrote a treatise whose title states the programme — on the difference between theoria and allegory — granting that a text may have a contemplative depth while denying that it may be made to mean what it does not say. This is the discipline of Neh 8:8, where the Levites “read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading,” and of Philip's question in Act 8:30, “Understandest thou what thou readest?” The honour is real: expository preaching as the church has known it at its best descends from Antioch and not from Alexandria. The defect is equally real and was inherited by his pupils — a reluctance to see Christ in the Old Testament where the New Testament plainly finds Him, and a Christology that kept the natures so distinct that the Person came apart.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to expound as to explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.
webster_full: EXPOUND', v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret; as, to expound a text of scripture.
2. To lay open; to examine.
LIT'ERAL, a. According to the letter; primitive; real; not figurative or metaphorical.
scriptures: Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Act 8:30
And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?
Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,

As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.
corruption_summary: Antioch was right about the letter and short on the Lord, and Alexandria was right about the Lord and reckless with the letter; the church needed both corrections and took neither cleanly.
corruption_paragraphs: The Antiochene instinct is the one this dictionary follows: the words mean what they say, and the expositor's first duty is to give the sense. Against the Alexandrian habit of finding the Trinity in a number and the soul's ascent in a place-name, Diodore was simply correct, and 2Pe 3:16 warns what becomes of those who “wrest” the Scriptures. But a method that will not receive the New Testament's own readings of the Old has stopped being literal and become selective, since the plainest fact about Psa 22 is the use the Gospels make of it.

The deeper failure was Christological and followed from the same temper. Holding the two natures firmly apart protected the true humanity and lost the unity of the Person, and from Diodore through Theodore to Nestorius the line runs straight. Chalcedon gave the settlement both schools needed: one Person in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation. The recovery is to take Antioch's discipline with Chalcedon's confession, reading the text as it stands and confessing the Christ the whole canon declares — for it was the risen Lord who “opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” (Luk 24:45).

“which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest” (2Pe 3:16) — the abuse he opposed.

pos: n. (Julian of Eclanum, c. 386–455, bishop of Eclanum in Apulia, the ablest defender of Pelagianism and Augustine's antagonist for twenty years)
etymology: Latin Julianus; Eclanum was a town of the Hirpini in southern Italy. Not Julian the Apostate, the emperor.
biblical_def: Julian of Eclanum was the son of a bishop, married in a wedding Paulinus of Nola celebrated in verse, and made bishop young. When Pelagianism was condemned he refused to subscribe, lost his see, and spent the rest of his life writing against Augustine, who answered him at enormous length in the unfinished Opus Imperfectum. Julian is the clearest of the Pelagians because he argued the premises openly. He held that Adam's sin injured only Adam; that infants are born in the state Adam was created in; that concupiscence is a natural good, part of the body God made; and that death is a condition of nature, not a penalty. He accused Augustine of Manichaeism for teaching otherwise, which was a shrewd charge against a former Manichee and a false one. Scripture decides it. “Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men” (Rom 5:12) makes Adam's act the entry of both sin and death for all. Psa 51:5 traces it to conception, Eph 2:3 calls us “by nature the children of wrath,” and Job 14:4 asks what Julian never answered: “Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines original sin, in theology, as the sin which is imputed to all men in consequence of the fall and transgression of Adam.
webster_full: ORIG'INAL, a. First in order; preceding all others.
ORIGINAL SIN, in theology, that sin which is imputed to all men, with its corruption of nature, in consequence of the fall and first transgression of Adam.
DEPRAV'ITY, n. A vitiated state; corruption of moral principles.
scriptures: Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
Psa 51:5
Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.
Eph 2:3
Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others.
Job 14:4
Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one.
corruption_summary: Julian is more modern than Augustine: his doctrine of the newborn child, of desire and of death is what most people in the West now assume without having read a word of him.
corruption_paragraphs: Pelagianism was condemned and then quietly won the popular mind. Julian's three theses — that children are born innocent, that desire is simply natural, and that death belongs to the constitution of things — are the default convictions of the modern West, including much of the evangelical West, and they are held without argument because they feel obvious. Scripture contradicts each. Psa 51:5 says “I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me,” which is a statement about origin, not about an unhappy childhood. Rom 5:12 makes death a wage. The doctrine of original sin is not a gloomy opinion about children; it is the reason the gospel must be monergistic.

The second corruption is the therapeutic reframing of Augustine's doctrine as damage to self-worth, so that the charge against him is now psychological rather than exegetical. That is Julian's charge in a new dress and it fails for the same reason: the question is not whether the doctrine is pleasant but whether Rom 5:12 and Eph 2:3 say it. They do. And the doctrine is in fact the only ground of comfort available, since a man who is “by nature” a child of wrath is saved by sovereign mercy and not by a capacity he was supposed to have and cannot find.

“I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psa 51:5) — against the innocent newborn.
“Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one” (Job 14:4) — the question he never answered.

pos: n. (Photius, c. 810–893, patriarch of Constantinople, the most learned Greek of his age, whose disputes with Rome produced the Photian schism and the formal Eastern rejection of the filioque)
biblical_def: Photius was a layman and imperial official raised to the patriarchate in 858 after his predecessor was deposed, which Rome refused to recognize. The quarrel that followed was about jurisdiction — who ruled the new Bulgarian church, and whether a pope could judge a patriarch — but Photius turned it into a doctrinal case by attacking the Western addition to the creed. The Latin church had come to say that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; Photius answered that the clause was added without a council, that it had no warrant in the Greek text of Joh 15:26, and that it introduced two principles into the Godhead. His Mystagogy is the foundation of every Eastern argument since. On the procedural point he was right: no see may amend an ecumenical creed by itself, and the manner of the addition was a usurpation. On the doctrine he was wrong, for Scripture calls the Spirit “the Spirit of his Son” (Gal 4:6) and “the Spirit of Christ” (Rom 8:9), and the Son says in Joh 16:7, “I will send him unto you.” His Bibliotheca, which summarizes hundreds of books now lost, remains one of the great treasures of learning.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines procession, in theology, as the emanation of the Holy Spirit; and to proceed as to issue or come forth, as from a source.
webster_full: PROCES'SION, n. The act of proceeding or issuing forth, as from a source.
In theology, the emanation of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son.
PROCEED', v.i. To issue or come forth, as from a source.
scriptures: But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me:
Joh 16:7
Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you.
Gal 4:6
And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father.
Rom 8:9
But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you. Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.
corruption_summary: Photius was right that Rome had no authority to amend the creed alone and wrong about what the amended creed said, and the East has kept the error with the grievance.
corruption_paragraphs: Two things must be held apart. The filioque entered the Western creed by regional usage and papal sanction rather than by an ecumenical council, and that is a real fault: a creed received by the whole church is not one see's property. Photius's procedural objection deserves the concession the West has rarely made. But the doctrine itself is scriptural. The Spirit is sent by the Son (Joh 16:7), is called the Spirit of the Son (Gal 4:6) and the Spirit of Christ (Rom 8:9), and the eternal procession answers to the temporal sending. Joh 15:26 says He “proceedeth from the Father” and in the same verse that Christ will send Him; it does not exclude the Son, and the Greek argument requires it to.

The second corruption is the ecumenical trade now commonly proposed, in which the West drops the clause to purchase reunion and calls the difference a matter of emphasis. Amo 3:3 asks whether two can walk together except they be agreed, and the question of how the Persons subsist is not an emphasis. The Reformed churches confess the filioque with the whole Western tradition, and the honest path is to defend it from Scripture rather than to barter it, while granting Photius his point that no bishop may rewrite the church's confession by himself.

“but if I depart, I will send him unto you” (Joh 16:7) — the Son sending.

pos: n. (Michael Cerularius, c. 1000–1059, patriarch of Constantinople, whose exchange of excommunications with the papal legates in 1054 fixed the division of East and West)
etymology: Greek Keroularios, probably from keros, wax, a family trade-name; Latinized Cerularius.
biblical_def: Michael Cerularius was an ambitious courtier turned patriarch who closed the Latin churches in Constantinople and had a treatise published against Western usages: unleavened bread at the Supper, fasting on Saturdays, the omission of the Alleluia in Lent, celibate clergy, and the filioque. Pope Leo IX sent legates under Cardinal Humbert, who were met with contempt; in July 1054 Humbert laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia and Cerularius anathematized the legates in return. Neither act in itself divided the churches — each struck at persons, not at the other see — but the hardening was permanent, and the sack of Constantinople by the Fourth Crusade in 1204 made it irreparable. The tragedy is that the occasion was largely ceremonial. 1Co 1:13 asks “Is Christ divided?” and Eph 4:4 confesses “one body, and one Spirit”; the leaven of the bread is not of that order. Where the real issues lay — the papal claim built on Mat 16:18, and the procession of the Spirit — they were scarcely argued, because two proud men were quarrelling about customs.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines schism as, in a general sense, division or separation; but appropriately, a division or separation in a church or denomination of Christians.
webster_full: SCHISM, n. In a general sense, division or separation; but appropriately, a division or separation in a church or denomination of christians, occasioned by diversity of opinions.
2. In Scripture, the breach of charity, which is the bond of the church.
scriptures: Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?
Eph 4:4
There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling;
That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.
And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
corruption_summary: The churches of East and West divided over bread, beards and the calendar while the doctrines that actually separated them went unexamined.
corruption_paragraphs: A division is not justified by the fact that it occurred, and 1054 is the standing example of a schism in which the stated grounds were largely indifferent things. Fasting days and the form of the bread belong to the liberty Rom 14 governs; they are not a cause for anathema. At the same time the deep issues were genuine and remain so: Rome's reading of Mat 16:18 as the charter of a universal monarchy over the church is an error the Reformation had to answer, and the rock on which Christ builds is the confession Peter had just made, not an office at Rome. Cerularius and Humbert fought over the wrong things and bequeathed the right ones unsettled.

The modern corruption runs the other way, into an ecumenism that treats every doctrinal difference as a ceremonial one and seeks reunion by agreeing not to ask. Joh 17:21 is the favourite text of that programme, and the prayer it records is that believers may be one “as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee” — a unity in truth, not a managed silence about it. The recovery is to divide over nothing indifferent and to concede nothing essential: refuse the anathema over leaven, and refuse the papacy over Mat 16:18.

pos: n. (Roscelin of Compiègne, c. 1050–c. 1125, the first great nominalist, whose application of nominalism to the Trinity was condemned as tritheism at Soissons in 1092)
etymology: Old French Roscelin, a Germanic diminutive; Latinized Roscelinus, of Compiègne.
biblical_def: Roscelin taught that universals are names only — that humanity is a word covering individual men and has no existence of its own. Applied to logic the thesis is defensible and became one of the two great medieval positions. Applied to the Godhead it was ruinous, and Roscelin applied it. If only individuals exist, and the Father, Son and Holy Ghost are three, then the divine substance they are said to share is a mere name, and there are three Gods. He seems to have pressed this as a question rather than a dogma, but the conclusion was plain and the Council of Soissons condemned it in 1092; Anselm of Canterbury wrote his treatise on the incarnation of the Word against him. The answer is the Shema itself: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4), with 1Jn 5:7, “these three are one,” and Isa 45:5, “I am the LORD, and there is none else.” Roscelin is also remembered as the first teacher of Peter Abelard, who took his master's logic, avoided his heresy, and fell into another.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines nominalism by way of the nominalists, a sect of school philosophers who maintained that universals are mere names or words.
webster_full: NOM'INALIST, n. One of a sect of school philosophers, the followers of Occam or Ockham, who maintained that universals have no real existence, but are mere names or words.
NOM'INAL, a. Titular; existing in name only; as a nominal distinction.
REALIST, n. One who maintains that universals have a real existence.
scriptures: Deu 6:4
Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:
For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.
Joh 14:9
Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father?
Isa 45:5
I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me: I girded thee, though thou hast not known me:
corruption_summary: Roscelin proves that a theory of language is never only that, and that a philosophy carried unexamined into theology will decide a doctrine before anyone notices.
corruption_paragraphs: The error was not that Roscelin reasoned badly within his system but that he let the system legislate for the Godhead. Nominalism answers a question about words; the Trinity is revealed, and the revelation includes both that God is one and that the Father, Son and Spirit are each that one God. When a philosophical commitment cannot carry both, the commitment yields. This is the permanent discipline for every theological use of a borrowed framework, and it applies as much to the modern borrowings — from psychology, sociology, process metaphysics — as to eleventh-century logic. “The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4) is not negotiable with a theory of universals.

The second corruption is the opposite excess the realists courted, and into which some Augustinians fell: making the divine essence a fourth thing in which the Persons participate, which is a quaternity. Scripture gives neither three Gods nor an essence behind the Persons. It gives one God subsisting in three Persons, each wholly God, distinguished by eternal relations and not by parts. Divine simplicity in the Reformed scholastic sense is the guard on both sides, and the Lord's own word to Philip settles the unity of operation and being: “he that hath seen me hath seen the Father” (Joh 14:9).
roots_summary: Hebrew echad (H259), one; Greek heis (G1520), one; ousia, substance or essence (the term at issue).

Greek heis (G1520) — one; 1 John 5:7.
Hebrew zulah (H2108) — besides, except; Isaiah 45:5.
Greek horao (G3708) — to see, to perceive; John 14:9.
Greek homoousios — of one substance, the word nominalism could not carry.
usage: “The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4) — the word his logic could not hold.
“and these three are one” (1Jn 5:7) — against tritheism.

pos: n. (the Synod of Whitby, 664, the Northumbrian conference at which King Oswiu decided for the Roman reckoning of Easter against the Celtic usage)
etymology: Old Norse Hvitabyr, the white settlement, on the Yorkshire coast; at the time called Streanaeshalch.
biblical_def: The Synod of Whitby settled a quarrel that had divided the Northumbrian church down the middle of the royal household: the king kept Easter by the Roman calculation and the queen by the Celtic, so that one fasted while the other feasted. Colman of Lindisfarne spoke for the Ionan tradition received from Aidan and, he claimed, from John the apostle; Wilfrid spoke for Rome and ended by appealing to Peter and the keys. Bede reports that Oswiu asked Colman whether Columba had been given the keys of the kingdom, and when Colman admitted he had not, the king decided for Rome. With the date went the form of the tonsure and, in time, the absorption of the Celtic churches into the Roman order. The matter in dispute was a calendar, and Scripture places calendars in the sphere of liberty: “Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday” (Col 2:16), and “One man esteemeth one day above another” (Rom 14:5). What was not indifferent was the ground of the decision, for a kingdom was turned on a reading of the keys.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council; an assembly of divines convened for consultation on matters of religion.
webster_full: SYN'OD, n. An ecclesiastical council; a meeting of bishops, or other ministers, convened for consultation on matters of religion.
2. A meeting or assembly in general.
3. In astronomy, a conjunction of two or more of the heavenly bodies.
scriptures: Col 2:16
Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days:
Rom 14:5
One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
Gal 4:10
Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Whitby decided an indifferent thing by an authority claim, and that is the shape of nearly every later imposition on the conscience.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors met at Whitby. The Celtic party made its calendar a mark of fidelity to a tradition; the Roman party made its calendar a test of submission to Peter's successor. Both treated an adiaphoron as weighty, and Gal 4:10 warns against the instinct — “Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years” — written to a church being brought back under bondage. The regulative principle cuts cleanly here: what Scripture commands in worship is required, what it has not commanded is not to be imposed, and a date of Easter is nowhere commanded. The Lord's Day is the Christian sabbath by apostolic practice; the annual calendar is not.

The graver matter is the argument that won. Oswiu was persuaded by a claim about the keys, and the church of the Angles was ordered by a conclusion drawn from Mat 16:19 as though the keys were a jurisdiction deposited at Rome. They are the authority Christ gave His church to bind and loose by His Word, exercised by the eldership of the congregation. The recovery is to settle indifferent things by the rule of 1Co 14:40 — “Let all things be done decently and in order” — and to settle nothing at all by an appeal to a see.
roots_summary: Greek heorte (G1859), a feast or holyday; krino (G2919), to judge; euschemonos (G2156), decently.

Greek krino (G2919) — to judge, to pass sentence; Colossians 2:16, Romans 14:5.
Greek paratereo (G3906) — to observe scrupulously; Galatians 4:10.
Greek euschemonos (G2156) — decently, becomingly; 1 Corinthians 14:40.
Greek taxis (G5010) — order, arrangement; 1 Corinthians 14:40.

“One man esteemeth one day above another” (Rom 14:5) — the apostolic ruling on calendars.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — how such a question should be settled.

pos: n. (the Council of Constance, 1414–1418, which ended the Great Western Schism of three rival popes, condemned Wycliffe posthumously, and burned John Hus in violation of an imperial safe-conduct)
etymology: Latin concilium, a calling together; Constance (Konstanz) on the lake at the Swiss and German border.
biblical_def: The Council of Constance met to end a scandal: three men each claimed to be pope, and each had obedient nations behind him. It succeeded, deposing two, accepting the resignation of the third, and electing Martin V. It also declared, in the decree Haec Sancta, that a general council holds authority immediately from Christ and that even a pope must obey it in matters of faith and reform — the conciliarist thesis, which Rome has never been able either to honour or to erase. And it burned a man. John Hus came under the Emperor Sigismund's written safe-conduct, was imprisoned on arrival, refused the right to defend his writings, and was handed to the secular arm on 6 July 1415 and burned; Jerome of Prague followed in 1416. The council's defence was that no faith need be kept with a heretic. Psa 94:20 asks whether “the throne of iniquity” shall have fellowship with God, “which frameth mischief by a law,” and that is precisely what was done at Constance — a judicial murder framed by a law.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a council as an assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice; and a general council, in church history, as a convention of the whole church.
webster_full: COUN'CIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
2. In ecclesiastical affairs, an assembly of prelates and doctors, convened for regulating matters of doctrine and discipline.
A general council is an assembly of ecclesiastics representing the whole church.
scriptures: Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?
Isa 5:20
Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: Constance healed a schism and broke a promise, and the church has spent six centuries explaining that the promise did not count.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine invoked at Constance — that no safe-conduct binds when a heretic is concerned — is a denial of the ninth commandment dressed as a canon, and Isa 5:20 names it: “Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil.” An oath is binding because God hears it, not because the man it was sworn to is sound. The council's real achievement, ending the papal schism, does not purchase the fire; and the burning of Hus did not end his cause but gave Bohemia a martyr and the Reformation a precedent, which is why Luther at Leipzig would say that Hus had been condemned for holding what Scripture teaches.

The second corruption is the use of Constance to argue that councils are the church's final court — conciliarism as the cure for papalism. It is not the cure, because a council may err as plainly as a pope, and this one did. The only final court is the Word of God, and the martyr's answer is the one the apostles gave: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29), spoken by men who had taken the measure of Mat 10:28 — “fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.”

pos: n. (the Council of Ferrara-Florence, 1438–1445, the attempted reunion of the Greek and Latin churches, signed by the Greeks under political duress and repudiated at Constantinople)
etymology: Latin concilium; opened at Ferrara in 1438 and moved to Florence in 1439 because of plague and the cost.
biblical_def: The Council of Ferrara-Florence was convened as the Ottoman armies closed on Constantinople. The Emperor John VIII came west in person with the patriarch and a large delegation, because reunion with Rome was the price of a crusade to save the city. For months the Greeks argued the filioque, purgatory, unleavened bread and the papal primacy; worn down, short of money, far from home and under the plainest political necessity, all but one signed the decree Laetentur Caeli in July 1439. The one was Mark of Ephesus, who refused and whom the East has honoured ever since. The union collapsed on contact with reality: the clergy and people of Constantinople rejected it, the promised help never came in force, and the city fell in 1453. It is the classic case of agreement purchased rather than reached. 2Co 6:14 governs the terms on which the church may unite, Amo 3:3 asks “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?”, and Jer 8:11 names the result: “they have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines union as the act of joining two or more things into one, and thus forming a single body; and concord as agreement between persons.
webster_full: UN'ION, n. The act of joining two or more things into one, and thus forming a compound body or a mixture.
2. Concord; agreement and conjunction of mind, will, affections or interest.
CON'CORD, n. Agreement between persons; union in opinions, sentiments, views or interests.
scriptures: Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
Amo 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Gal 2:5
To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.
Jer 8:11
For they have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
corruption_summary: Florence is the proof that a union signed under necessity is not a union, and that the churches which trade doctrine for help get neither.
corruption_paragraphs: The Greeks did not change their minds at Florence; they changed their signatures. Reunion was the condition of military aid, and a confession produced by that pressure bound nobody, which the reception at home immediately showed. The permanent lesson is about the nature of agreement: it is the mind persuaded from Scripture, or it is nothing. Gal 2:5 shows the apostle refusing to give place “by subjection, no, not for an hour” where the truth of the gospel was at stake, and he was under pressure too. Every ecumenical instrument since has had to reckon with Florence, which is why honest dialogue begins by asking what has actually been believed, not what can be signed.

The second corruption is the modern treatment of Mark of Ephesus's refusal as mere obstinacy, the one man who would not be reasonable while a city burned. He has the better of it. If the filioque and the papal primacy are what each side said they were, then no emergency makes them negotiable, and a man who signs what he does not believe has lied in the name of peace. The Reformed answer is not Rome's and not the East's, but the method is Mark's: hold what Scripture proves, decline what it does not, and refuse to buy concord with a false subscription.
